images.title: A winning chain in Hex
images.purpose: Shows the goal of Hex on a small board: an unbroken chain of one colour joining that player's two sides.
images.composition: A small rhombus shaped board of 9 hexagon cells, large and centred, with coloured edges for each player and one highlighted chain. Plain white background, lots of empty space around the main object, no scenery, no people, no extra text.
images.exact_structure: A rhombus board of 3 rows of 3 flat topped hexagon cells; each row is shifted half a cell to the right of the row above. Name the cells row by row, left to right: row 1 cells A, B, C; row 2 cells D, E, F; row 3 cells G, H, I (these letters are not drawn). The top and bottom edges of the board have a thick teal (#0072B2) bar; the left and right edges have a thick amber (#E69F00) bar. Teal pieces fill B, E and H, forming a chain from the top edge to the bottom edge (B touches E, E touches H); the chain is outlined in reddish purple (#CC79A7) with the label 'winning chain' beside it. Amber pieces fill D and F. Cells A, C, G and I are empty white. The label 'Player 1' sits next to the top teal bar and 'Player 2' next to the left amber bar. Exactly 9 cells: 3 teal, 2 amber, 4 empty.
rejection: any count of objects, cells, ticks or rows that differs from the numbers stated in the spec
any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
a hyphen used in place of a minus sign on any labelled number
images.takeaway: In Hex you win by joining your two sides with one unbroken chain.
images.description: Shows the goal of Hex on a small board: an unbroken chain of one colour joining that player's two sides.
images.context: Rhombus Hex: row r shifted right by half a cell per row, so (r, c) touches (r + 1, c); B, E, H are cells (0, 1), (1, 1), (2, 1).
images.teaching_notes: Teal moved first, so 3 teal against 2 amber pieces is a legal position.

image_decisions.why: The rule of Hex is visual; one small board with a winning chain explains it at a glance.
